result: The ARM device was designed and built using linear stages, cameras, and stimulus holders to deliver mechanical stimuli to mouse paws with improved accuracy and consistency. The ARM decreased off-target distance by 93.3% compared to manual delivery and delivered more consistent stimulus based on high-speed videography analysis.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7 provide quantitative experimental evidence showing 93.3% improvement in targeting accuracy and improved consistency via high-speed video analysis. Claims C42, C46-C50 describe the technical design and capabilities of the device, which are factual descriptions of the system construction. The convergence of design specifications and performance data supports this result.

result: The ARM device does not induce stress in mice due to its operational noise, as demonstrated by open field testing showing no significant differences in locomotion or anxiety-related behaviors when the ARM was running versus silent.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 report statistical analysis (Student's t-test) of open field test measures showing no significant differences in multiple behavioral parameters. C51 provides observational context that ARM noise was minimal compared to background HVAC. The statistical testing with appropriate controls supports the conclusion that ARM noise does not induce stress.

result: The ARM delivers von Frey filament stimuli with greater accuracy, consistency, and speed compared to manual delivery by experienced researchers. The ARM had no variation in stimulus delivery time whereas manual delivery showed 12.4-61.17% variation, and reduced testing time by 50.9%. However, significant inter-researcher variability was observed in manual delivery but eliminated when using the ARM remotely.
evaluation: Claims C10-C13 provide quantitative measurements of force application accuracy, temporal consistency, and speed improvements with appropriate statistical comparisons. Claims C14-C15 demonstrate that manual delivery produces significant inter-researcher variability (p=0.0008) that is eliminated with ARM use. The convergence of multiple performance metrics with statistical support validates this result.

result: The ARM successfully validated mechanical pain assays in inflammatory pain models (carrageenan and CFA), detecting hypersensitivity through decreased withdrawal latency to noxious stimuli, decreased mechanical threshold, and increased affective behaviors. Catch trials confirmed responses were stimulus-driven rather than noise-driven.
evaluation: Claims C16-C19 and C61-C63 provide statistical evidence (t-tests, ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.05) demonstrating the ARM can detect pain-related behavioral changes in established inflammatory pain models. C19 and C63 show catch trial controls with 96% true response rate vs 7% false positive rate, validating that responses are stimulus-specific. C64 appropriately infers reliability across sexes. The combination of positive results in pain models with appropriate controls supports this validation result.

result: Mice habituate more quickly to experimental conditions when no experimenter is present, as demonstrated by remote-habituated mice showing significantly decreased time to rest and reduced turning behavior compared to mice habituated with a researcher present.
evaluation: Claims C20-C22 provide statistical evidence (two-way ANOVA, p<0.05) showing remote-habituated mice exhibited faster habituation across multiple behavioral measures. C23 appropriately interprets these findings in the biological context of mice as prey animals. The statistical support with appropriate comparisons validates this experimenter effect on habituation.

result: Experimenter presence causes significant sex-dependent differences in both reflexive and affective pain behaviors that appear and disappear depending on which researcher is present and their sex. Male researchers induced significantly decreased mechanical threshold in female vs male mice, while individual researchers produced variable effects on paw withdrawal features.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 provide statistical evidence (two-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.05) demonstrating experimenter-dependent and sex-dependent effects on multiple behavioral measures. C27 specifically shows male researchers produce sex-dependent effects (p=0.034) that don't occur with female researchers. C28 and C44 appropriately synthesize these findings. The pattern of results across multiple researchers and behavioral measures supports this conclusion about experimenter effects.

result: Stimulus intensity variability significantly affects reflexive behavioral responses (withdrawal latency, max paw height) more than affective responses (shaking, distance traveled). Reflexive features showed significant correlations explaining 13.8-26.9% of variance, while affective features showed weak or no correlation with stimulus intensity.
evaluation: Claims C29-C30 provide linear regression analysis showing differential effects of stimulus intensity on reflexive vs affective features with quantified variance explained (R²). C31 and C65 appropriately interpret these findings. C66 contextualizes the importance by noting that commonly used pain measures are based on reflexive responses. The statistical analysis with appropriate methodology supports the differential effect conclusion.

result: The ARM successfully integrates with in vivo calcium imaging to link mechanical stimuli, BLA neural activity, and pain behaviors at sub-second resolution. BLA neurons showed stimulus-specific regulation, with 29.3% regulated by pain, 10.7% by touch, and 11.4% by both. Neural activity correlated more strongly with affective behavioral measures (paw distance traveled, max y-velocity) than traditional reflexive measures (withdrawal latency).
evaluation: Claims C32-C34 demonstrate successful detection of stimulus-evoked neural responses with appropriate statistical analysis (peri-event analysis, Wilcoxon rank-sum). Claims C35-C36 show Pearson correlations between neural activity and behavior with quantified variance explained (8.54-13.88%). C37-C38 appropriately interpret the utility of different behavioral metrics. Claims C45, C67-C68 provide context from prior work. The convergence of neural recording, behavioral analysis, and statistical correlations supports this integration result.

result: The PAWS analysis software was updated and validated to work with lower-cost 500 fps cameras (vs 2000 fps), showing no significant differences in measured features and sufficient discrimination between cotton swab and pinprick responses. Software improvements included graphical interface, SLEAP tracking compatibility, and ARM integration.
evaluation: Claim C52 provides statistical validation (two-way ANOVA) showing equivalence between 500 fps and 2000 fps data. C53 demonstrates functional validation by distinguishing stimulus types. C54-C55 describe factual software improvements. The statistical validation combined with functional demonstration supports the lower-cost camera validation result.

result: A new force sensor-guided stimulus was developed to overcome von Frey filament limitations, providing two modes: force ramp (0.5-8g over 5s) and consistent force with velocity adjustment. The system automatically detects paw withdrawal and reports mechanical threshold and withdrawal latency.
evaluation: Claim C56 provides observational motivation for the innovation. Claims C57-C60 describe the technical capabilities of the force sensor system, which are factual descriptions of the device functionality validated through the pain model experiments (C17-C18, C61-C62). The technical description combined with successful validation in pain models supports this innovation result.

result: The manuscript establishes the scientific context for developing the ARM by citing prior work on rodent pain models, experimenter effects, existing device limitations, brain regions involved in pain, and applications beyond pain research.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5, C39-C41, and C70 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These claims establish the scientific rationale and context for the study but do not represent new findings from the current work. The citations appear appropriate for establishing background knowledge.

result: The ARM democratizes pain research by reducing training requirements, improving accessibility for researchers with physical disabilities, and has been commercialized through Tactorum Inc for widespread adoption.
evaluation: Claims C69 and C71 make interpretive statements about broader impact that, while reasonable inferences from the demonstrated capabilities, are not directly tested in the study. C72 is a factual statement about commercialization. The accessibility and democratization claims are plausible but represent aspirational goals rather than demonstrated outcomes.

result: The manuscript describes experimental methods including animal care, device operation, behavioral assays, surgical procedures, imaging parameters, and data analysis workflows in accordance with institutional guidelines.
evaluation: Claims C73-C89 are factual statements about methods, procedures, and compliance with regulations. These are standard methodological descriptions that support reproducibility. C73 specifically documents IACUC approval. These claims describe how the work was conducted rather than representing results.
